title: The burden of proof is inverted for ACs: they must clearly and convincingly prove their own alignment
content:
A.1.5.9.0.4.2 is the Atlas's most explicit statement on burden allocation: "Facilitators are not to assume innocence or give leeway in cases of ambiguity. Instead, the burden is on the Alignment Conserver to provide clear and convincing evidence of their alignment. Any uncertainty or doubt regarding the AC's alignment will be resolved against them, requiring them to definitively prove their adherence to the Atlas."

Three distinct reversals are stacked here. The presumption is removed (no assumed innocence), the burden is moved onto the accused, and the standard imposed on that burden is elevated — "clear and convincing," a demanding threshold, and "definitively prove."

The rationale traces to Alignment Artifact Strength: the whole point of these roles is that the ecosystem can rely on them without verifying each act, and reliance is only safe if the burden of demonstrating trustworthiness sits with the trusted party. Voluntary assumption of the role is what makes it defensible — nobody is compelled to be an AC.

There is a real tension with A.1.5.4.0.4.1, which sets the facilitator's finding threshold at "51% or greater chance that the AC committed a misaligned act." Read together, misalignment is *found* on a bare majority of likelihood, while exculpation requires *clear and convincing* proof. These are asymmetric standards operating on the same question, and no provision reconciles them. The practical effect is a wide band of genuine ambiguity in which the AC loses under both rules simultaneously — which appears to be intended rather than accidental, given how consistently the Governance Scope resolves doubt against whoever holds power.

NR-5 registers the discomfort directly, asking whether "'fairness' is not an objective in any proceeding involving AC derecognition. What are the arguments for and against this?"
description: A.1.5.9.0.4.2 forbids assuming innocence or granting leeway in ambiguity, requiring the AC to definitively prove adherence — sitting uneasily beside the 51% finding threshold.
